claim: PIM1 protein was strongly induced within 3 hr of TCR engagement in naive OT1 CD8 T cells.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics analysis of naive OT1 CD8 T cell stimulated with their cognate peptide over time (Marchingo et al., 2020) showed that PIM1 protein was strongly induced within 3 hr of TCR engagement, which was sustained at a 24-hr time point (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data from a published dataset showing PIM1 protein levels over time, and is visualized in Figure 1A.

claim: PIM1 protein expression was sustained at 24 hr post-TCR engagement in OT1 CD8 T cells.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics analysis of naive OT1 CD8 T cell stimulated with their cognate peptide over time (Marchingo et al., 2020) showed that PIM1 protein was strongly induced within 3 hr of TCR engagement, which was sustained at a 24-hr time point (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data showing sustained PIM1 expression at 24 hr, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PIM2 expression was not detected until 9 hr post-TCR stimulation in OT1 CD8 T cells.
source: PIM2 expression was not detected until 9 hr post-stimulation but was also sustained at the 24-hr time point.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data from the time course experiment described in the manuscript.

claim: PIM2 protein expression was sustained at 24 hr post-TCR stimulation in OT1 CD8 T cells.
source: PIM2 expression was not detected until 9 hr post-stimulation but was also sustained at the 24-hr time point.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing sustained PIM2 expression at 24 hr.

claim: 24-hr polyclonal activation of CD8 T cells with αCD3/αCD28 agonist antibodies induced expression of PIM1 and PIM2 proteins.
source: 24-hr polyclonal activation of CD8 T cells with αCD3/αCD28 agonist antibodies similarly induced expression of PIM1 and PIM2 proteins (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing PIM1 and PIM2 protein levels after 24 hr activation, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Increases in PIM1 and PIM2 protein expression at 24 hr post-activation were underpinned by transcriptional reprogramming.
source: These increases in PIM kinase expression at a protein level were underpinned by transcriptional reprograming, with both Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA very lowly expressed in naive CD8 T cells and strongly upregulated by immune activation (Figure 1C; Spinelli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing increased Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA levels after activation, as shown in Figure 1C and cited from a published dataset.

claim: Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA are very lowly expressed in naive CD8 T cells.
source: These increases in PIM kinase expression at a protein level were underpinned by transcriptional reprograming, with both Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA very lowly expressed in naive CD8 T cells and strongly upregulated by immune activation (Figure 1C; Spinelli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data from a published dataset showing low Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA levels in naive cells.

claim: Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA are strongly upregulated by immune activation in CD8 T cells.
source: These increases in PIM kinase expression at a protein level were underpinned by transcriptional reprograming, with both Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA very lowly expressed in naive CD8 T cells and strongly upregulated by immune activation (Figure 1C; Spinelli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing increased mRNA levels after activation.

claim: Pim1 and Pim2 are the major PIM kinases in T cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports of Pim1 and Pim2 being the major PIM kinases in T cells (Mikkers et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2005), Pim3 mRNA was only expressed at very low levels in naive and activated CD8 T cells (Figure 1C), with PIM3 protein not detected at all by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq and proteomics data showing low/absent Pim3 expression, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Pim3 mRNA was only expressed at very low levels in naive and activated CD8 T cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports of Pim1 and Pim2 being the major PIM kinases in T cells (Mikkers et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2005), Pim3 mRNA was only expressed at very low levels in naive and activated CD8 T cells (Figure 1C), with PIM3 protein not detected at all by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing low Pim3 mRNA levels.

claim: PIM3 protein was not detected by mass spectrometry in naive and activated CD8 T cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports of Pim1 and Pim2 being the major PIM kinases in T cells (Mikkers et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2005), Pim3 mRNA was only expressed at very low levels in naive and activated CD8 T cells (Figure 1C), with PIM3 protein not detected at all by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing absence of PIM3 protein.

claim: PIM1 and PIM2 have similar substrate selectivity and functional redundancy.
source: PIM1 and PIM2 have similar substrate selectivity and hence functional redundancy (Mikkers et al., 2004; Bullock et al., 2005; Fox et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007; Warfel and Kraft, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple literature citations establishing this property of PIM kinases.

claim: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice.
source: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) similar to what has been reported previously in Pim dKO mice on an FVB/N genetic background (Mikkers et al., 2004), although the total number of T cells and splenocytes was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type (WT) mouse spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing T cell proportions in spleens, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: The total number of T cells in Pim dKO mouse spleens was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type mouse spleens.
source: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) similar to what has been reported previously in Pim dKO mice on an FVB/N genetic background (Mikkers et al., 2004), although the total number of T cells and splenocytes was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type (WT) mouse spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced total T cell numbers in Pim dKO spleens.

claim: The total number of splenocytes in Pim dKO mice was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type mice.
source: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) similar to what has been reported previously in Pim dKO mice on an FVB/N genetic background (Mikkers et al., 2004), although the total number of T cells and splenocytes was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type (WT) mouse spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced total splenocyte numbers.

claim: The reduced total number of T cells and splenocytes in Pim dKO mice was likely the result of these mice being smaller in size.
source: This was not attributable to any one cell type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; James et al., 2021) but was instead likely the result of these mice being smaller in size, a phenotype that has previously been reported in Pim1/2/3 triple KO mice (Mikkers et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and comparison with previous literature showing smaller size in PIM-deficient mice.

claim: Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells showed a normal increase in cell size in response to in vitro immune activation with αCD3/αCD28 agonist antibodies.
source: We tested how Pim dKO T cells respond to immune activation and observed a normal increase in cell size in response to in vitro immune activation with αCD3/αCD28 agonist antibodies (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing FSC-A SSC-A profiles in Figure 1D.

claim: 24 hr αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells normally upregulated expression of CD25, CD44 and CD71.
source: 24 hr αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells also normally upregulated expression of established markers of T cell activation including CD25, CD44 and the transferrin receptor CD71 (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing activation marker expression in Figure 1E.

claim: 24 hr TCR-activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells produced normal levels of IFNγ.
source: 24 hr TCR-activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells also produced normal levels of the key effector cytokine IFNγ (Figure 1E) and there was no discernible difference in TCR-driven proliferation between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture (Figure 1F and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing IFNγ production in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no discernible difference in TCR-driven proliferation between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture.
source: 24 hr TCR-activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells also produced normal levels of the key effector cytokine IFNγ (Figure 1E) and there was no discernible difference in TCR-driven proliferation between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture (Figure 1F and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by CTV proliferation assay data shown in Figures 1F and 1J.

claim: High-resolution mass spectrometry quantified expression of >7000 proteins in 24 hr αCD3/αCD28 activated WT and Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells.
source: These experiments quantified expression of >7000 proteins but found no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition in activated WT versus Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells (Figure 1G–H) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing the number of proteins quantified.

claim: There were no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition in 24 hr activated WT versus Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells.
source: These experiments quantified expression of >7000 proteins but found no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition in activated WT versus Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells (Figure 1G–H) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing minimal differences between genotypes, as shown in Figures 1G-H.

claim: PIM kinases do not play an important unique role in the signalling pathways used by the TCR and CD28 to control T cell activation.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that PIM kinases do not play an important unique role in the signalling pathways used by the TCR and CD28 to control T cell activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing no substantial differences in activation markers, proliferation, or proteome composition between WT and Pim dKO T cells.

claim: A previous study reported that Pim dKO naive T cells cultured in IL-7 died in response to rapamycin treatment.
source: This previous study showed Pim dKO, but not WT, naive T cells cultured in IL-7 died in response to rapamycin treatment.
evidence: The claim references findings from a previous study (Fox et al., 2005).

claim: A previous study showed that rapamycin synergised with Pim1/Pim2-deficiency to substantially reduce TCR-driven activation and proliferation.
source: It was also shown that rapamycin synergised with Pim1/Pim2-deficiency to substantially reduce TCR-driven activation and proliferation (Fox et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim references findings from a previous study.

claim: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of naive CD8 T cells cultured with IL-7 to survive in response to rapamycin treatment.
source: However, we found no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of naive CD8 T cells cultured with IL-7 to survive in response to rapamycin treatment (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There was no difference in the effect of rapamycin on mean division number in αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO versus WT CD8 T cells.
source: Furthermore, we found no difference in the effect of rapamycin on mean division number in αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO versus WT CD8 T cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: PIM 1 and PIM2 are rapidly and strongly expressed in response to immune activation.
source: Collectively, these data show that PIM 1 and PIM2 are rapidly and strongly expressed in response to immune activation, but they are dispensable for the antigen receptor and CD28-driven proteome remodelling that initiates T cell clonal expansion and differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics and RNAseq data showing rapid induction of PIM kinases after activation.

claim: PIM1 and PIM2 are dispensable for the antigen receptor and CD28-driven proteome remodelling that initiates T cell clonal expansion and differentiation.
source: Collectively, these data show that PIM 1 and PIM2 are rapidly and strongly expressed in response to immune activation, but they are dispensable for the antigen receptor and CD28-driven proteome remodelling that initiates T cell clonal expansion and differentiation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing no substantial differences in proteome composition or activation phenotypes between WT and Pim dKO T cells.

claim: There is no evidence that mTORc1 was substituting for Pim1 and Pim2 loss in TCR-activated T cells.
source: We also found no evidence that mTORc1 was substituting for Pim1 and Pim2 loss.
evidence: The claim is based on the rapamycin experiments showing no differential effect in Pim dKO versus WT cells.

claim: IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells.
source: In this context, PIM1 and PIM2 kinase expression is regulated by the cytokines IL-2 and IL-15 which are key to shaping CD8 T cell effector and memory cell differentiation, respectively (Weninger et al., 2001; Cornish et al., 2006; Buck et al., 2016). Both IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells (Figure 2A) and are required to sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression (Rollings et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: IL-2 and IL-15 are required to sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells.
source: Both IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells (Figure 2A) and are required to sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression (Rollings et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and a literature citation.

claim: PIM1 and PIM2 mediate IL-15 induced proliferation of gut intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IEL).
source: Previous work has shown that PIM1 and PIM2 mediate IL-15 induced proliferation of gut intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IEL; James et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim references findings from a previous study.

claim: Antigen experienced WT CD8 T cells show an ~90-fold expansion between days 2 and 6 of culture in IL-15.
source: Antigen experienced WT CD8 T cells show a robust proliferative response to IL-15 such that there is an ~90-fold expansion of the CD8 T cells between days 2 and 6 of culture (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Immune activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells showed a moderate proliferative disadvantage in IL-15, resulting in an ~4-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of culture.
source: Immune activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells also proliferated strongly in response to IL-15, but showed a moderate proliferative disadvantage resulting in an ~4-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of the culture (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-15 to sustain CD8 T cell viability.
source: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-15 to sustain CD8 T cell viability (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 unique polyA+ RNA in IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells.
source: The RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 unique polyA+ RNA and using a cut off of >1.5 fold-change and q-value <0.05 we saw that the abundance of 381 polyA+ RNA was modified by Pim1/Pim2-deficiency (Figure 2E) (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing the number of RNA quantified.

claim: The abundance of 381 polyA+ RNA was modified by Pim1/Pim2-deficiency in IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (FC >1.5, q<0.05).
source: The RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 unique polyA+ RNA and using a cut off of >1.5 fold-change and q-value <0.05 we saw that the abundance of 381 polyA+ RNA was modified by Pim1/Pim2-deficiency (Figure 2E) (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing differentially expressed RNA.

claim: Only 72 substantially expressed protein coding mRNA were differentially expressed in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
source: Of the 381 RNA that were detected as differentially expressed (FC >1.5, q<0.05) only ~30% were detected with an average expression over 10 transcripts per million (TPM), of these gene ~36% were non-coding RNA, uncharacterised genes or pseudogenes, leaving only 72 substantially expressed protein coding mRNA that were differentially expressed in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of RNAseq data filtering for expression level and gene type.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency has very little effect on IL-15 induced protein-coding mRNA expression in differentiated T cells.
source: These data indicate that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency has very little effect on IL-15 induced protein-coding mRNA expression in differentiated T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RNAseq data showing only 72 substantially expressed protein-coding mRNA were differentially expressed.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not decrease expression of mRNA levels for CD62L (Sell), Ccr7 and S1pr1 in IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
source: We found that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not decrease expression of mRNA levels for critical memory T cell genes such as the adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors, Sell (CD62L), Ccr7 and S1pr1 that direct the trafficking of CD8 T cells to secondary lymphoid tissue. (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not reduce expression of mRNA for the key memory cell transcription factors Tcf7, Foxo1, Foxo3, Klf2, and Id3 in IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
source: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency also did not reduce expression of mRNA for the key memory cell transcription factors Tcf7, Foxo1, Foxo3 Klf2, and Id3. (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There were small increases in expression of Klf2, Id3, and Ccr7 mRNA in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
source: Indeed, if anything, there were small increases in expression of the Klf2, Id3, and Ccr7 mRNA in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: Proteomics analysis quantified expression of ~6900 total proteins in IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells.
source: Critically, when the proteomes of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were analysed and expression of ~6900 total proteins quantified, there were no major changes in the proteomes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Figure 2H, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing the number of proteins quantified.

claim: There were no major changes in the proteomes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
source: Critically, when the proteomes of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were analysed and expression of ~6900 total proteins quantified, there were no major changes in the proteomes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Figure 2H, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The mitochondrial proteome composition of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were indistinguishable.
source: Of note, the mitochondrial proteome composition of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were indistinguishable (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing mitochondrial protein expression in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: IL-15 controls memory T cells via mitochondrial remodelling to support energy production via oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation.
source: This is pertinent because one key feature of how IL-15 controls memory T cells is via mitochondrial remodelling to support energy production via oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation (Buck et al., 2016), and it has been described that PIM kinases can control mitochondrial phenotypes in cancer cell lines and cardiomyocytes (Din et al., 2013; Chauhan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations describing IL-15's role in mitochondrial remodelling.

claim: PIM kinases can control mitochondrial phenotypes in cancer cell lines and cardiomyocytes.
source: This is pertinent because one key feature of how IL-15 controls memory T cells is via mitochondrial remodelling to support energy production via oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation (Buck et al., 2016), and it has been described that PIM kinases can control mitochondrial phenotypes in cancer cell lines and cardiomyocytes (Din et al., 2013; Chauhan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: PIM1 and PIM2 do not drive IL-15-mediated metabolic or differentiation programs in antigen-primed CD8 T cells.
source: These data show that PIM1 and PIM2 do not drive IL-15-mediated metabolic or differentiation programs in antigen-primed CD8 T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics and RNAseq data showing minimal differences between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded cells.

claim: The copy numbers per cell of PIM1 protein is considerably higher in actively expanding antigen-activated CD8 cells maintained with IL-2 compared to IL-15.
source: IL-2 promotes the expression of PIM1 and PIM2 kinases (Figure 2A), and in this context, we noted that the copy numbers per cell of PIM1 protein is considerably higher in actively expanding antigen-activated CD8 cells maintained with IL-2 compared to IL-15 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pim dKO antigen activated CD8 T cells responded normally to IL-2 to induce STAT5 Y694 phosphorylation.
source: The data show that Pim dKO antigen activated CD8 T cells responded normally to IL-2 to induce STAT5 Y694 phosphorylation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pim dKO CD8 T cells express normal levels of CD25 (IL-2-receptor alpha chain).
source: They also express normal levels of the IL-2-receptor alpha chain, CD25, (Figure 3C), which is sustained by STAT5.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Antigen activated WT CD8 T cells have an ~270-fold expansion between days 2 and 6 of culture in saturating IL-2 concentrations.
source: Antigen activated WT CD8 T cells have a strong survival and proliferative response to IL-2 producing an ~270-fold expansion between days 2 and 6 of culture in saturating IL-2 concentrations (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-2 to maintain CD8 T cell viability.
source: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-2 to maintain CD8 T cell viability (Figure 3E) and Pim dKO cells CD8 T cells cultured in IL-2 proliferated robustly.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pim dKO CD8 T cells cultured in IL-2 exhibited a very mild proliferative disadvantage resulting in an ~2-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of culture.
source: They did however exhibit a very mild proliferative disadvantage resulting in an ~2-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of the culture (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of activation markers CD44 and CD71 in IL-2-expanded CTL were similar between WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells on days 3 and 6 of co-cultures.
source: Expression of activation markers CD44 and CD71 in IL-2-expanded CTL were similar between WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells on days 3 and 6 of co-cultures (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: WT CTL downregulated expression of CD62L in IL-2, whereas Pim dKO CTL sustained higher CD62L expression.
source: However, one consistent difference between IL-2 maintained WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells is that WT CTL downregulated expression of CD62L (L-selectin, Sell), whereas the Pim dKO CTL sustained higher CD62L expression (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL were smaller and less granular than the corresponding WT CTL.
source: We also noted that IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL had reduced forward and side scatter properties, revealing that they were smaller and less granular than the corresponding WT CTL (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing FSC-A and SSC-A in Figure 3F.

claim: Proteomics analysis quantified expression of ~6900 proteins in day 6 IL-2 cultured WT and Pim dKO CTL.
source: These analyses quantified expression of ~6900 proteins and showed a small decrease in the total protein mass of IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells compared to WT cells (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing the number of proteins quantified.

claim: There was a small decrease in the total protein mass of IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells compared to WT cells.
source: These analyses quantified expression of ~6900 proteins and showed a small decrease in the total protein mass of IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells compared to WT cells (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 513 proteins were down-regulated (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
source: The data showed down-regulation of the expression of 513 proteins (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL along with increased copy numbers of 33 proteins (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 33 proteins had increased copy numbers (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
source: The data showed down-regulation of the expression of 513 proteins (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL along with increased copy numbers of 33 proteins (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The transcription factor profile of Pim dKO T cells was consistent with that of an effector CTL with high levels of TBX21 and low levels of TCF1.
source: The transcription factor profile of Pim dKO T cells was consistent with that of an effector CTL with high levels of TBX21 and low levels of TCF1 (Tcf7; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pim dKO T cells exhibited an effector-like mitochondrial proteome profile.
source: Pim dKO T cells also exhibited an effector-like mitochondrial proteome profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pim dKO CTL had lower levels of the glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 compared to WT CTL.
source: These included lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (GLUT1 and GLUT3; Figure 4D) which are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions (Chang et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4D and is consistent with previous literature on glucose transporter function.

claim: SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells.
source: These included lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (GLUT1 and GLUT3; Figure 4D) which are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions (Chang et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Glucose transporters are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions.
source: These included lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (GLUT1 and GLUT3; Figure 4D) which are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions (Chang et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Pim dKO CTL had decreased expression of proteins involved in fatty acid and cholesterol biosynthesis including SCD2, HMGCS1, MVK, IDI1, FDPS, FDFT1, and SQLE.
source: Pim dKO CTL also had decreased expression of a number of proteins involved in fatty acid and cholesterol biosynthesis including SCD2, HMGCS1, MVK, IDI1, FDPS, FDFT1, and SQLE (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Pim dKO CD8 cells had reduced levels of multiple granzymes, perforin, IFNγ, and TNFα.
source: Another striking observation was that the Pim dKO CD8 cells had reduced levels of a number of key effector proteins including multiple granzymes, perforin, IFNγ, and TNFα (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figures 4F-H.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed reduced levels of Granzyme B and IFNγ in IL-2 expanded Pim dKO CTL.
source: Orthogonal flow cytometric analysis of Granzyme B and IFNγ levels confirmed reduced levels of these effector molecule in IL-2 expanded Pim dKO CTL, although IFNγ protein is only lowly produced in IL-2 maintained CTL (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: 24 hr treatment with pan-PIM kinases inhibitors PIM447 or AZD1208 caused reductions in cell proliferation, cell size, cell granularity, fatty acid biosynthesis proteins SCD1-3, glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3, and Granzyme B expression in IL-2 maintained WT CTL.
source: When IL-2 maintained WT CTL were treated for 24 hr with the pan-PIM kinases inhibitors PIM447 or AZD1208 we saw reductions in cell proliferation, cell size, cell granularity, fatty acid biosynthesis proteins SCD1-3, glucose transporters SLC2A1, SLC2A3 and a reduction in Granzyme B expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–E, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics and flow cytometry data from PIM kinase inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pattern of proteome remodelling in Pim dKO CTL had some phenotypic features in common with previously reported changes following inhibition of mTORc1 in CTL.
source: The pattern of proteome remodelling in Pim dKO CTL had some phenotypic features in common with the previously reported changes that occur following inhibition of the Serine/Threonine kinase mTORc1 in CTL (Hukelmann et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019). These included: increased expression of PDCD4 and decreased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes and effector molecules including granzymes, perforin, IFNγ and TNFα (Hukelmann et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current proteomics data with previous literature on mTORc1 inhibition effects.

claim: mTORc1 activity in CTL is acutely sensitive to reduced availability of glucose.
source: In this respect, mTORc1 activity in CTL is acutely sensitive to reduced availability of glucose (Rolf et al., 2013) and the reduced expression of glucose transporters in Pim dKO T cells might predict that these cells would have lower activity of mTORc1.
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency modestly reduced mTORc1 activity in IL-2 maintained CD8 T cells.
source: These data show a modest reduction of mTORc1 activity in the Pim dKO T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing reduced pS6K T389 in Figure 6A.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency reduced IL-2 induced mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation of S6 in CD8 T cells.
source: These data also show that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency reduced IL-2 induced mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation of S6 but did not compromise the ability of the Pim dKO cells to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores; pharmacological activators that induce RSK mediated S6 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced pS6 in Pim dKO cells in Figure 6B.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not compromise the ability of CD8 T cells to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores.
source: These data also show that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency reduced IL-2 induced mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation of S6 but did not compromise the ability of the Pim dKO cells to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores; pharmacological activators that induce RSK mediated S6 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing normal pS6 response to PdBU/ionomycin in Pim dKO cells in Figure 6B.

claim: Decreased glucose availability or inhibition of mTORc1 prevents the downregulation of CD62L that normally accompanies IL-2-induced CTL differentiation.
source: Previously, it has been shown that decreased glucose availability or inhibition of mTORc1 prevents the downregulation of CD62L that normally accompanies IL-2-induced CTL differentiation (Sinclair et al., 2008; Finlay et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: CD62L (Sell) mRNA expression is increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
source: The IL-2 CTL transcriptomics data showed there is increased expression of CD62L at the mRNA level in IL-2 maintained PimdKO CTL (Figures 5B and 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 5B and 6C.

claim: The expression of Sell (CD62L) mRNA is controlled by the transcription factor KLF2.
source: The expression of Sell (CD62L) mRNA is controlled by the transcription factor KLF2 and the expression of Klf2 mRNA is also increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL (Figure 6D) as are mRNA levels for other KLF2 targets: the chemokine receptors Ccr7 and S1pr1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of transcriptional regulation and is supported by RNAseq data.

claim: Klf2 mRNA expression is increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
source: The expression of Sell (CD62L) mRNA is controlled by the transcription factor KLF2 and the expression of Klf2 mRNA is also increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL (Figure 6D) as are mRNA levels for other KLF2 targets: the chemokine receptors Ccr7 and S1pr1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: mRNA levels for Ccr7 and S1pr1 are increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
source: The expression of Sell (CD62L) mRNA is controlled by the transcription factor KLF2 and the expression of Klf2 mRNA is also increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL (Figure 6D) as are mRNA levels for other KLF2 targets: the chemokine receptors Ccr7 and S1pr1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CD62L/L-selectin controls T cell adhesion to the endothelium of high endothelial venules and is essential for lymphocyte transit from blood into secondary lymphoid tissue.
source: CD62L/L-selectin controls T cell adhesion to the endothelium of high endothelial venules and is essential for lymphocyte transit from blood into secondary lymphoid tissue such as lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of CD62L function.

claim: CCR7 and S1P1 receptor direct migration by controlling T cell entry and egress respectively into secondary lymphoid tissue.
source: CCR7, and the S1P1 receptor also direct migration by controlling T cell entry and egress respectively into secondary lymphoid tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of chemokine receptor function.

claim: The loss of CD62L, CCR7 and S1PR1 expression following immune activation reprograms the trafficking of effector T cells away from lymphoid tissue toward sites of inflammation in peripheral tissues.
source: In this context, the loss of CD62L, CCR7 and S1PR1 expression following immune activation reprograms the trafficking of effector T cells away from lymphoid tissue toward sites of inflammation in peripheral tissues (Sinclair et al., 2008; Nolz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Pim dKO CTL, but not WT CTL, retained substantial capacity to home to secondary lymphoid organs and accumulated in lymph nodes and spleen after adoptive transfer.
source: Figure 6E shows that Pim dKO CTL, but not WT CTL, retained substantial capacity to home to secondary lymphoid organs and, hence, accumulated in lymph nodes and spleen: PIM kinases are thus required for the normal reprogramming of CTL trafficking.
evidence: The claim is supported by adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PIM kinases are required for the normal reprogramming of CTL trafficking.
source: Figure 6E shows that Pim dKO CTL, but not WT CTL, retained substantial capacity to home to secondary lymphoid organs and, hence, accumulated in lymph nodes and spleen: PIM kinases are thus required for the normal reprogramming of CTL trafficking.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the adoptive transfer data showing differential homing between WT and Pim dKO CTL.

claim: The loss of PIM kinases had no effect on the CD8 T cell programs controlled by antigen receptor/co-stimulation.
source: The loss of PIM1 and PIM2 was shown to have no effect on the CD8 T cell programs controlled by antigen receptor/co-stimulation and had very little impact on the IL-15-driven transcriptional and proteomic programs in memory differentiated CD8 T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics and phenotyping data showing no substantial differences in TCR-activated Pim dKO versus WT cells.

claim: The loss of PIM kinases had very little impact on the IL-15-driven transcriptional and proteomic programs in memory differentiated CD8 T cells.
source: The loss of PIM1 and PIM2 was shown to have no effect on the CD8 T cell programs controlled by antigen receptor/co-stimulation and had very little impact on the IL-15-driven transcriptional and proteomic programs in memory differentiated CD8 T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RNAseq and proteomics data showing minimal differences in IL-15 expanded Pim dKO versus WT cells.

claim: PIM1 and PIM2 were required for IL-2 programming of effector CD8 T cell differentiation.
source: However, PIM1 and PIM2 were required for IL-2 programming of effector CD8 T cell differentiation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics and phenotyping data showing multiple differences in IL-2 expanded Pim dKO versus WT CTL.

claim: IL-2 controls essential cytolytic effector and metabolic programs in CTL.
source: IL-2 controls essential cytolytic effector and metabolic programs in CTL, is a key cytokine for CD8 T cell anti-viral immunity and is also used to produce cytotoxic T cells for anti-cancer immunotherapy (Kalia and Sarkar, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: PIM kinases mediate IL-2 control of the expression of glucose transporters, lipid metabolic enzymes and key cytolytic proteins in effector CD8 T cells.
source: The understanding that PIM kinases mediate IL-2 control of the expression of glucose transporters, lipid metabolic enzymes and key cytolytic proteins such as granzymes A and B in effector CD8 T cells is thus fundamental information about how this key cytokine controls T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics data showing reduced expression of these proteins in Pim dKO CTL.

claim: PIM kinases did not control the transcriptional programs that direct expression of glucose transporters and effector enzymes.
source: It was also important to understand that PIM kinases did not control the transcriptional programs that direct expression of glucose transporters and effector enzymes and hence the full consequences of PIM kinase deletion could only be assessed by in depth analysis of the proteomes of Pim1/Pim2-deficient CTL and not from mRNA sequencing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined RNAseq and proteomics data showing discordance between mRNA and protein changes.

claim: The loss of PIM kinase activity reduced protein synthesis rates in CTL.
source: The loss of PIM kinase activity reduced protein synthesis rates in CTL which explains the discordance between mRNA and protein reported herein.
evidence: The claim is supported by OPP incorporation data showing reduced protein synthesis after PIM kinase inhibitor treatment.

claim: The reduction in protein synthesis in Pim dKO CTL was modest.
source: The reduction in protein synthesis was modest but previous studies have shown that modest reductions in protein synthesis and loss of mTORc1 activity impact CD8 T cell differentiation programs (Cornish et al., 2006; Hukelmann et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on the OPP incorporation data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: PIM kinase regulation of protein translation has been reported previously in mouse B cell lymphoma and mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: PIM kinase regulation of protein translation has been reported previously in mouse B cell lymphoma and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Schatz et al., 2011) and some of the key examples of proteins we found to be unaltered at the mRNA level but down-regulated at the protein level have prior reports of sensitivity to translational regulation in immune cells (Fehniger et al., 2007; Ricciardi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Reduced protein synthesis capacity in cells lacking PIM kinases could be caused by reduced mTORc1 activity combined with increased expression of the translational repressor PDCD4.
source: Reduced protein synthesis capacity in cells lacking PIM kinases could be caused by reduced mTORc1 activity combined with increased expression at the mRNA and protein level of the translational repressor PDCD4.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics, RNAseq, and mTORc1 activity data.

claim: Protein synthesis is highly energetically demanding.
source: Moreover, protein synthesis is highly energetically demanding and once CTL have reduced glucose transporter expression this would reduce glucose availability to fuel protein production.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: PIM kinases are required for IL-2 to fully repress expression of CD62L, CCR7, and S1PR1 in effector CD8 T cells.
source: One other important insight from the current work is that PIM kinases are required for IL-2 to fully repress expression of the adhesion molecule CD62L and the chemokine receptors CCR7 and S1PR1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RNAseq and flow cytometry data showing increased expression of these molecules in Pim dKO CTL.

claim: CD62L, CCR7, and S1PR1 play a key role in controlling T cell homing to secondary lymphoid tissue.
source: These molecules play a key role in controlling T cell homing to secondary lymphoid tissue and are expressed at high levels in naive and memory T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of these molecules' functions.

claim: IL-2 induces down regulation of CD62L, CCR7, and S1PR1 expression as part of a program that causes effector cells to lose their capacity to home to secondary lymphoid tissues.
source: IL-2 induces down regulation of CD62L, CCR7, and S1PR1 expression as part of a program that causes effector cells to lose their capacity to home to secondary lymphoid tissues (Sinclair et al., 2008; Nolz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: PIM kinases can mediate IL-2 repression of lymph node homing receptors and the ability of IL-2 to switch off the naive T cell trafficking program.
source: The present data show that PIM kinases can mediate this IL-2 repression of lymph node homing receptors and the ability of IL-2 to switch off the naive T cell trafficking program.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing retained expression of homing receptors and lymph node homing capacity in Pim dKO CTL.

claim: IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 effector T cells retain the capacity to home to secondary lymphoid tissues in vivo.
source: IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 effector T cells thus retain the capacity to home to secondary lymphoid tissues in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by adoptive transfer data showing Pim dKO CTL accumulation in lymph nodes and spleen.

claim: The loss of PIM kinases does not cause IL-2 differentiated effector T cells to differentiate instead into memory cells.
source: This lymph-node homing pattern is also a memory CD8 T cell phenotype but here it is pertinent that the current in-depth analysis of the transcriptomes and proteomes of Pim1/Pim2-deficient IL-2 differentiated CD8 T cells show that the loss of PIM kinases does not cause effector T cells to differentiate instead into memory cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics and RNAseq data showing effector-like characteristics in Pim dKO CTL.

claim: IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells do not re-express key molecules that maintain the stem-like properties of memory cells such as TCF7 and IL-7 receptor.
source: For example, IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells do not re-express key molecules that maintain the stem-like properties of memory cells such as the transcription factor TCF7 and IL-7 receptor (Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics and RNAseq data showing low expression of these memory markers.

claim: Pim dKO CTL cultured in IL-2 do not have the mitochondrial proteome of a memory T cell.
source: Nor do Pim dKO CTL cultured in IL-2 have the mitochondrial proteome of a memory T cell and PCA plots of IL-15 and IL-2 proteomics and RNAseq data show that Pim dKO IL-2 expanded CTL are still much more similar to IL-2 expanded WT CTL than to IL-15 expanded CTL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data and PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency prevents optimal differentiation of effector CTL but does not cause these cells to fully switch to a memory phenotype.
source: Hence Pim1/Pim2-deficiency prevents optimal differentiation of effector CTL but does not cause these cells to fully switch to a memory phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined proteomics and RNAseq data.

claim: Pan-PIM kinase inhibitors are in development as anti-cancer drugs.
source: This is worth knowing as pan-PIM kinase inhibitors are in development as anti-cancer drugs and it has been suggested that PIM inhibitors might be used as a strategy to generate more stem-memory-like CD8 T cells in combination with cancer immunotherapy treatments (Chatterjee et al., 2019; Clements and Warfel, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: It has been suggested that PIM inhibitors might be used as a strategy to generate more stem-memory-like CD8 T cells in combination with cancer immunotherapy treatments.
source: This is worth knowing as pan-PIM kinase inhibitors are in development as anti-cancer drugs and it has been suggested that PIM inhibitors might be used as a strategy to generate more stem-memory-like CD8 T cells in combination with cancer immunotherapy treatments (Chatterjee et al., 2019; Clements and Warfel, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: The selectivity of PIM kinases for IL-2 control of conventional CD8 T cell differentiation with no evidence that PIMs were important for IL-15 responses beyond a modest effect on cell proliferation was interesting.
source: Finally, the selectivity of PIM kinases for IL-2 control of conventional CD8 T cell differentiation with no evidence that PIMs were important for IL-15 responses beyond a modest effect on cell proliferation was interesting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing differential effects of PIM kinase loss in IL-2 versus IL-15 conditions.

claim: The failure to see a role for PIM signalling in conventional peripheral CD8 T cell differentiation is in contrast to observations that PIM1 and PIM2 direct IL-15 control of the metabolic programming of intestinal IEL.
source: This failure to see a role for PIM signalling in conventional peripheral CD8 T cell differentiation is in contrast to observations that PIM1 and PIM2 direct IL-15 control of the metabolic programming of intestinal IEL (James et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current data with previous literature.

claim: In IEL, IL-15 was being used individually to drive immune activation and was sufficient to strongly induce PIM1 and PIM2 expression.
source: A notable difference between these scenarios was that in IEL, IL-15 was being used individually to drive immune activation and was sufficient to strongly induce PIM1 and PIM2 expression.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous literature on IEL.

claim: In conventional CD8 T cells, IL-15 does not sustain high levels of PIM kinases.
source: In contrast, in our conventional CD8 T cell system we uncovered that IL-15 does not sustain high levels of PIM kinases, which could possibly explain this discrepancy.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing lower PIM kinase levels in IL-15 versus IL-2 expanded cells.

claim: High levels of PIM expression alone are not inevitably predictive of their importance.
source: However, high levels of PIM expression alone are not inevitably predictive of their importance. In this study, we observed very high levels of both PIM1 and PIM2 in antigen activated CD8 T cells yet loss of PIM kinases there had no functional impact.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing high PIM expression but no functional impact in TCR-activated cells.

claim: PIM kinases were required to maximally stimulate mTORc1 activity in IL-2 expanded CTL.
source: Previously, it was suggested that mTORc1 could compensate for PIM kinase deficiency (Fox et al., 2005). However, we found no evidence for this, and in fact observed that PIM kinases were required to maximally stimulate mTORc1 activity in IL-2 expanded CTL.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and flow cytometry data showing reduced mTORc1 activity in Pim dKO CTL.

claim: This examination of the role of PIM kinases in multiple signalling situations reveal cell context-dependent regulatory roles for PIM kinases rather than hard wired functions that apply to every stimulatory situation in T cells.
source: Thus, this examination of the role of PIM kinases in multiple signalling situations reveal cell context-dependent regulatory roles for PIM kinases rather than hard wired functions that apply to every stimulatory situation in T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing differential effects of PIM kinase loss across different stimulation conditions.

claim: RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 polyA+ RNA in IL-2 expanded WT and Pim dKO CTL.
source: In these experiments, ~14,000 polyA+ RNA were quantified and using a cut off >1.5 fold-change, q<0.05 we saw that the abundance of 223 mRNA were decreased and 155 increased by Pim1/Pim2 deficiency (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing the number of RNA quantified.

claim: The abundance of 223 mRNA were decreased and 155 increased by Pim1/Pim2 deficiency in IL-2 expanded CTL (FC >1.5, q<0.05).
source: In these experiments, ~14,000 polyA+ RNA were quantified and using a cut off >1.5 fold-change, q<0.05 we saw that the abundance of 223 mRNA were decreased and 155 increased by Pim1/Pim2 deficiency (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing differentially expressed mRNA.

claim: The reduced expression of perforin and Granzymes C-G and K protein corresponded to decreases in their mRNA in Pim dKO CTL.
source: These data revealed that the reduced expression of perforin and Granzymes C-G and K protein corresponded to decreases in their mRNA (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined RNAseq and proteomics data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: A clear decrease in Granzymes B and A protein levels did not correspond with an appreciable decrease in mRNA expression in Pim dKO CTL.
source: However, there were striking examples where a clear decrease in protein levels did not correspond with an appreciable decrease in mRNA expression. These included the predominant cytolytic Granzymes B and A (Figure 5C and D), as well as both glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined RNAseq and proteomics data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: A clear decrease in glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 protein levels did not correspond with an appreciable decrease in mRNA expression in Pim dKO CTL.
source: However, there were striking examples where a clear decrease in protein levels did not correspond with an appreciable decrease in mRNA expression. These included the predominant cytolytic Granzymes B and A (Figure 5C and D), as well as both glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined RNAseq and proteomics data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ~75% of the proteins whose expression was changed in Pim dKO CTL (FC >1.5, q<0.05) exhibited no strong corresponding changes in their mRNA (FC <1.2).
source: Furthermore, contrasting differential expression of proteins and mRNA data in Pim dKO vs WT CTL revealed that ~75% of the proteins whose expression was changed in Pim dKO T cells (FC >1.5, q<0.05), exhibited no strong corresponding changes in their mRNA (FC <1.2; Figure 5F, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined RNAseq and proteomics data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Of the ~500 proteins whose expression decreased at the protein level in Pim dKO CTL only 17 showed a strong decrease in magnitude at the mRNA level as well.
source: Indeed, of the ~500 proteins whose expression decreased at the protein level in Pim dKO CTL only 17 showed a strong decrease in magnitude at the mRNA level as well (Figure 5G, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined RNAseq and proteomics data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There was a small reduction in ribosome protein content in Pim dKO CTL, which scaled with the reduction in total protein content.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we observed a small reduction in ribosome protein content in Pim dKO CTL, which scaled with the reduction in total protein content (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The translational repressor PDCD4 was increased in Pim dKO CTL.
source: Moreover, the translational repressor PDCD4 was increased in Pim dKO CTL (Figure 5I). This could be confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 5J) and was underpinned at the mRNA level (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics, flow cytometry, and RNAseq data shown in Figures 5I, 5J, and 5B.

claim: 24 hr inhibition with pan PIM kinases inhibitors was sufficient to substantially increase PDCD4 protein expression.
source: Similarly, 24 hr inhibition with pan PIM kinases inhibitors was sufficient to substantially increase PDCD4 protein expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data from PIM kinase inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: There was a small decrease in the expression of EIF4A1 in Pim dKO IL-2 maintained CTL.
source: We also noted that there was a small decrease in the expression of EIF4A1, a key component of the eIF4F translation initiation complex, in Pim dKO IL-2 maintained CTL (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: PDCD4 inhibits translation by binding EIF4A1 in a 2:1 ratio, preventing its interaction with the EIF4F complex.
source: PDCD4 inhibits translation by binding EIF4A1 in a 2:1 ratio, preventing its interaction with the EIF4F complex (Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation describing the mechanism of PDCD4 action.

claim: The changes in PDCD4 and EIF4A1 protein levels equated to an approximate halving of the ratio between EIF4A1 and PDCD4 in Pim dKO CTL.
source: Together the changes in both proteins equated to an approximate halving of the ratio between EIF4A1 and PDCD4 (Figure 5L).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data and calculation shown in Figure 5L.

claim: 24 hr of treatment with pan-PIM kinase inhibitors PIM447 or AZD1208 caused a quantitative reduction in protein synthesis rates of IL-2 expanded CTL.
source: We found that 24 hr of treatment with pan-PIM kinase inhibitors PIM447 or AZD1208 caused a quantitative reduction in protein synthesis rates of IL-2 expanded CTL (Figure 5M).
evidence: The claim is supported by OPP incorporation data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: PIM kinase effects on protein expression are via control of protein translation.
source: This data is consistent with PIM kinase effects on protein expression being via control of protein translation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the protein synthesis data and the discordance between mRNA and protein changes.

claim: CD8 T cells express ~200 Serine/Threonine protein kinases.
source: CD8 T cells express ∼200 Serine/Threonine protein kinases (Navarro et al., 2014; Howden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: PIM kinases are constitutively active.
source: As PIM kinases are constitutively active, their participation in signalling cascades is dictated by regulated changes in their protein expression levels (Warfel and Kraft, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: PIM1 and PIM2 have little to no expression in naïve T cells but are induced by T-cell receptor activation and costimulation.
source: PIM1 and PIM2 have little to no expression in naïve T cells but are induced by T-cell receptor activation and costimulation (e.g. CD27) (Wingett et al., 1996; Fox et al., 2005; Peperzak et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations and is consistent with the data in the manuscript.

claim: PIM kinases are direct transcriptional targets of JAK/STAT signalling pathways.
source: PIM kinases are also direct transcriptional targets of JAK/STAT signalling pathways and as such PIM1 and/or PIM2 are rapidly induced in T cells downstream of a diverse array of cytokines, including multiple common cytokine receptor γ-chain family cytokines, IL-6 and IL-12 (Matikainen et al., 1999; Aho et al., 2005; Fox et al., 2005; Warfel and Kraft, 2015; Buchacher et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: A mild reduction in Pim1/Pim2/Pim3-deficient CD4 and CD8 T cell proliferation has been observed in response to sub-optimal TCR stimulation and IL-2.
source: A mild reduction in Pim1/Pim2/Pim3-deficient CD4 and CD8 T cell proliferation has been observed in response to sub-optimal TCR stimulation and IL-2 (Mikkers et al., 2004), and there is evidence that PIM1 and PIM2 control survival pathways in naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells in concert with mTORc1 (Fox et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: There is evidence that PIM1 and PIM2 control survival pathways in naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells in concert with mTORc1.
source: A mild reduction in Pim1/Pim2/Pim3-deficient CD4 and CD8 T cell proliferation has been observed in response to sub-optimal TCR stimulation and IL-2 (Mikkers et al., 2004), and there is evidence that PIM1 and PIM2 control survival pathways in naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells in concert with mTORc1 (Fox et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Pim1/Pim2/Pim3 deletion is reported to promote expression of stemness and memory-associated transcription factors including Bcl6 and Tcf7.
source: Pim1/Pim2/Pim3 deletion is reported to promote expression of stemness and memory-associated transcription factors including Bcl6 and Tcf7 (Chatterjee et al., 2019), and PIM kinase activity has been linked with maintenance of memory CD8 T cell survival (Knudson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: PIM kinase activity has been linked with maintenance of memory CD8 T cell survival.
source: Pim1/Pim2/Pim3 deletion is reported to promote expression of stemness and memory-associated transcription factors including Bcl6 and Tcf7 (Chatterjee et al., 2019), and PIM kinase activity has been linked with maintenance of memory CD8 T cell survival (Knudson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Pim1/Pim2 deficiency prevented mTORc1 activation and the proliferation of non-conventional intra-epithelial gut CD8 T lymphocytes (IEL) in response to IL-15.
source: It has also been shown recently that Pim1/Pim2 deficiency prevented mTORc1 activation and the proliferation of non-conventional intra-epithelial gut CD8 T lymphocytes (IEL) in response to the cytokine IL-15 (James et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Elevated PIM kinase expression has been noted in patient T cells for rheumatoid arthritis, uveitis and coeliac disease.
source: Elevated PIM kinase expression has been noted in patient T cells for a number of autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, uveitis and coeliac disease, and PIM kinase inhibition has been proposed as a possible intervention to dampen autoimmunity (James et al., 2021; Maney et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: PIM kinase inhibition has been proposed as a possible intervention to dampen autoimmunity.
source: Elevated PIM kinase expression has been noted in patient T cells for a number of autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, uveitis and coeliac disease, and PIM kinase inhibition has been proposed as a possible intervention to dampen autoimmunity (James et al., 2021; Maney et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: PIM kinase inhibitors have entered clinical trials to treat some cancers including multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukaemia, and prostate cancer.
source: PIM kinase inhibitors have also entered clinical trials to treat some cancers (e.g. multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukaemia, prostate cancer), and although they have not been effective as a monotherapy, there is interest in combining these with immunotherapies.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of clinical trials and is stated in the manuscript.

claim: PIM kinase inhibitors have not been effective as a monotherapy for cancer.
source: PIM kinase inhibitors have also entered clinical trials to treat some cancers (e.g. multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukaemia, prostate cancer), and although they have not been effective as a monotherapy, there is interest in combining these with immunotherapies.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of clinical trial outcomes.

claim: Studies show PIM inhibition reducing expression of inhibitory molecules (e.g. PD-L1) on tumour cells and macrophages in the tumour microenvironment.
source: This is due to studies showing PIM inhibition reducing expression of inhibitory molecules (e.g. PD-L1) on tumour cells and macrophages in the tumour microenvironment and a reported increase of stem-like properties in PIM-deficient T cells which could potentially drive longer lasting anti-cancer responses (Chatterjee et al., 2019; Xin et al., 2021; Clements and Warfel, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: PIM kinase inhibition has generally been shown to be inhibitory for T cell activation, proliferation, and effector activities.
source: However, PIM kinase inhibition has also generally been shown to be inhibitory for T cell activation, proliferation, and effector activities (Fox et al., 2003; Mikkers et al., 2004; Jackson et al., 2012) and use of PIM kinase inhibitors could have the side effect of diminishing the anti-tumour T cell response.
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.
